sections.b: A young prophet sent by Elisha anoints Jehu in a back room at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 9:1–10), and the army proclaims him king. Jehu shoots Joram on Naboth's land, has Ahaziah of Judah struck down, and has Jezebel thrown from a window at Jezreel (2 Kings 9:14–37). He tricks Samaria's nobles into beheading Ahab's seventy sons, kills forty-two princes of Judah, and lures Baal's worshipers into their temple to be slaughtered (2 Kings 10:1–28). The LORD promises him four generations on the throne, but he keeps Jeroboam's calves (2 Kings 10:29–31).

Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk shows Jehu, or his envoy, bowing to the ground, with a caption naming "Jehu son of Omri" and his tribute of silver, gold and vessels in 841 BC. The Tel Dan stele has an Aramean king, probably Hazael, claim to have killed Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, which some scholars read as a sign that Jehu acted as Hazael's ally. Kings mentions neither.

Jehu's house lasted about ninety years: Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II and Zechariah, murdered after six months, "so came true the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu" (2 Kings 15:12). Hosea, who preached under Jeroboam II, names his son Jezreel because God will visit "the blood of Jezreel" on Jehu's house (Hosea 1:4). Interpreters have explained the tension as Jehu exceeding his commission, as his later sins turning his bloodshed into guilt, or as two biblical voices judging the same events differently.

common: Jehu was God's chosen instrument to punish Ahab's house for Naboth's murder and for Baal worship.
"Driving like Jehu" (2 Kings 9:20, KJV "furiously") became an English byword for reckless driving.
uncommon: Some scholars think Jehu was Hazael's ally or vassal, so that the Tel Dan stele and Kings describe the same revolt from two sides.
A few historians have taken "son of Omri" on the Black Obelisk literally, making Jehu a member of a side branch of Omri's family.

claude.title: A revolt told with open eyes
claude.body: My reading is that the narrator of 2 Kings 9–10 deliberately shows Jehu's methods in detail, the double-edged letter (10:6), the spin to the crowd (10:9) and the lie to Baal's servants (10:19), so that the reader can admire the outcome without trusting the man. The closing verdict, that Jehu "took no care to walk with his whole heart" (10:31), then reads less as an afterthought than as the point the whole story has been preparing.

sections.b: Jehu charges Jezebel with "prostitution" and "sorceries," the prophets' words for idolatry (2 Kings 9:22). When he reaches Jezreel she paints her eyes, dresses her hair and taunts him from the window as "Zimri, who killed his master" (2 Kings 9:30–31). Her servants throw her down, Jehu tramples her, and when the men go to bury her, the dogs have left only her skull, feet and hands, as Elijah had said (2 Kings 9:33–37; 1 Kings 21:23). Popular belief reads her makeup as seduction; many commentators read it as a queen meeting death with dignity.

common: Jezebel painted her face to seduce Jehu.
A "Jezebel" is a scheming, immoral woman.
uncommon: Many modern commentators read Jezebel's makeup and taunt as the defiance of a queen who knew she would die.

sections.b: 2 Kings 9–10 carries out Elijah's sentence on Ahab (1 Kings 21:21–24). His son Joram is shot and thrown onto Naboth's land, his widow Jezebel is eaten by dogs, his seventy sons are beheaded in Samaria, and everyone left of his house in Jezreel and Samaria is killed (2 Kings 9:24–26; 2 Kings 10:1–11, 17). Through his daughter Athaliah, Ahab's line also nearly destroyed David's (2 Kings 11:1). The last verdict on Israel says the people "sold themselves to do evil," the phrase once used of Ahab alone (2 Kings 17:17; 1 Kings 21:25).

Elijah does not appear in these chapters, but his words drive them. Jehu claims he heard Elijah's oracle against Ahab in Naboth's vineyard (2 Kings 9:25–26), quotes the prophecy about the dogs and Jezebel (2 Kings 9:36–37), and says after each massacre that the LORD has done what he said "by his servant Elijah" (2 Kings 10:10, 17). One of the three anointings given to Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:15–16) is carried out here by a disciple of his successor.

Elisha's last political act is to send a young prophet to anoint Jehu (2 Kings 9:1–3), fulfilling the task given to Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19:16). The prophet who had named Hazael king of Aram (2 Kings 8:13) thus also sets in motion the revolt that ends Ahab's house.

Some forty years later the dying Elisha receives King Jehoash, who weeps over him with Elisha's own cry for Elijah, "My father! My father!" (2 Kings 13:14; 2 Kings 2:12). Elisha has the king shoot "an arrow of the LORD's saving help" toward Aram and strike the ground, and is angry that he stops at three (2 Kings 13:15–19). After his burial, a dead man thrown into his grave comes to life when he touches Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:20–21), an episode Ben Sira praised (Sirach 48:13–14) and church fathers used to defend honoring relics.

sections.h: Baal destroyed in Israel and Judah
sections.b: Jehu lures Baal's prophets, priests and worshipers into the house of Baal in Samaria with the promise of a great sacrifice, then has them killed and turns the temple into a latrine (2 Kings 10:18–28). In Judah, after Athaliah's fall, the people tear down a house of Baal in Jerusalem and kill its priest Mattan (2 Kings 11:18). Yet the Asherah pole still stands in Samaria (2 Kings 13:6), and the final verdict on Israel includes serving Baal (2 Kings 17:16). Inscriptions from Kuntillet 'Ajrud of about 800 BC bless "by YHWH of Samaria and his asherah."

Hazael of Aram, whom Elisha foresaw as Israel's scourge (2 Kings 8:12), takes Israel's lands east of the Jordan (2 Kings 10:32–33), captures Gath and turns toward Jerusalem until Joash pays him off (2 Kings 12:17–18), and reduces Israel's army to ten chariots (2 Kings 13:3, 7, 22). The Tel Dan stele is probably his. His son Ben-hadad, named "Bar-hadad son of Hazael" on the Zakkur stela, loses towns to Jehoash (2 Kings 13:24–25). Damascus finally falls to Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC after Ahaz asks for Assyria's help; Rezin is killed and the people are deported to Kir (2 Kings 16:5–9).

Assyria enters Kings with "Pul," the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III, who takes a thousand talents from Menahem (2 Kings 15:19–20). Tiglath-pileser's annals list "Menahem of Samaria" and "Jehoahaz (Ahaz) of Judah" among his tributaries and claim that he made Hoshea king after the Israelites overthrew Pekah. In 734–732 BC he took Galilee and Gilead and deported their people (2 Kings 15:29), then took Damascus at Ahaz's request (2 Kings 16:7–9). His son Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria (2 Kings 17:3–5), and Sargon II claimed its conquest and the deportation of 27,290 people (2 Kings 17:6). Kings reads Assyria as the LORD's instrument (2 Kings 17:18–23).

common: Assyria was the first empire to destroy one of the two Israelite kingdoms.
uncommon: Some historians think the Bible's picture of Assyrian pressure to adopt foreign worship, as in Ahaz's altar (2 Kings 16:10–18), was mostly Judah's own choice rather than Assyrian policy.

sections.b: When Jehu kills her son Ahaziah, Athaliah destroys the royal family and rules Judah for six years (2 Kings 11:1–3). Jehosheba, daughter of King Jehoram and perhaps Athaliah's stepdaughter, hides the infant Joash in the temple. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada crowns Joash with the help of the royal guard; Athaliah tears her clothes and cries "Conspiracy!" and is taken out and killed at the horses' entrance to the palace (2 Kings 11:4–16). The people then destroy the house of Baal in Jerusalem (2 Kings 11:18).

Jean Racine's tragedy Athalie (1691), Handel's oratorio Athalia (1733) and Mendelssohn's music for Racine's play made the hidden king and the fall of the queen one of the best-known Old Testament stories in Europe.

common: Athaliah was as wicked as Jezebel, who is usually taken to be her mother.
uncommon: Some scholars suggest Athaliah acted to protect herself and the Omride party in Judah after Jehu's purge, and that the account comes only from her enemies' side.

sections.b: Jehu's revolt in 841 BC is a fixed point, since Shalmaneser III received his tribute that year (2 Kings 10:34). After it the figures grow harder. Jehoahaz's seventeen years (2 Kings 13:1) and Jehoash's accession in Joash's thirty-seventh year (2 Kings 13:10) do not add up; Azariah's accession in Jeroboam's twenty-seventh year (2 Kings 15:1) conflicts with 2 Kings 14:17, 23; Pekah's twenty years (2 Kings 15:27) cannot fit Assyrian records of Menahem's tribute about 738 and Pekah's death by 732; and Hoshea's accession is dated both to Jotham's twentieth year and to Ahaz's twelfth (2 Kings 15:30; 2 Kings 17:1). Thiele and Galil use co-regencies, a rival kingdom for Pekah in Gilead, and changes in counting methods; Thiele admitted that 2 Kings 17:1 and 18:1 are twelve years off. Tadmor and Cogan, and Albright before them, treat some figures as errors and give Pekah about five years. Hayes and Hooker reject co-regencies and allow for scribal error. The puzzle is not solved.

sections.h: High places under the good kings of Judah
sections.b: Even the kings Kings praises in these chapters, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah and Jotham, leave the high places standing, and the formula repeats: "Only, the high places were not removed. The people were still sacrificing and burning offerings at the high places" (2 Kings 12:3; 2 Kings 14:4; 2 Kings 15:4; 2 Kings 15:35). Ahaz himself sacrifices there (2 Kings 16:4), and the verdict on Israel lists high places "from the lookout's tower to the walled city" (2 Kings 17:9). After 722 the settlers in Samaria install their own gods in Israel's old high-place shrines (2 Kings 17:29–32).

sections.h: The end of the northern kingdom
sections.b: 2 Kings 17 closes the story of the two kingdoms that began with Jeroboam (1 Kings 12). The narrator traces Israel's fall back to that day: the LORD tore Israel from David's house, and Jeroboam drove Israel away from following the LORD (2 Kings 17:21–22). "None were left except the tribe of Judah by itself" (2 Kings 17:18). Archaeology suggests that many northerners fled south, and Jerusalem grew greatly in the late eighth century BC.

Jehu's purge reaches Samaria, where Ahab's sons are beheaded and Baal's temple destroyed (2 Kings 10:1–28). The Asherah pole remains there (2 Kings 13:6). Menahem marches on Samaria from Tirzah, and Pekah kills Pekahiah in its citadel (2 Kings 15:14, 25). Shalmaneser V besieges it for three years, and it falls in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5–6). Assyria resettles its towns with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim (2 Kings 17:24), and Samaria becomes an Assyrian province.

sections.h: 2 Kings 17 and the Samaritans' own story
sections.b: Jewish tradition read 2 Kings 17:24–41 as the origin of the Samaritans and called them Kutim, after Cuthah. Josephus calls them Cuthaeans (Antiquities 9.288–291), and the Talmud debates whether they were true converts or "lion converts" (Bavli Kiddushin 75b; 2 Kings 17:25). The word Shomronim in 2 Kings 17:29 means the Israelite people of Samaria, not the later community. The Samaritans call themselves Shamerim, "keepers" of the Law, descendants of Ephraim and Manasseh, and date the schism to Eli's move from Gerizim to Shiloh. Modern historians generally think the separation took shape much later, with both northern Israelite and foreign roots.

Chronicles tells that during the war of Pekah and Rezin, men of Ephraim, at the word of the prophet Oded, clothed, fed and anointed their Judean captives, put the weak on donkeys and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:8–15). Many readers have seen this as a background to Jesus' parable of the Samaritan on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30–37).

Kings records two Assyrian deportations of Israelites: from Galilee and Gilead under Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:29) and from Samaria after its fall, to Halah, the Habor River of Gozan and the towns of Media (2 Kings 17:6). The narrator explains it as the LORD removing Israel "out of his sight" for breaking the covenant, "as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets" (2 Kings 17:18–23), and warns that Judah walks the same road (2 Kings 17:19).

Kings ends its account of Israel with the words "Israel went into exile from its own soil to Assyria, and is there to this day" (2 Kings 17:23). The Mishnah records a debate: Rabbi Akiva said the ten tribes would not return, citing Deuteronomy 29:28, while Rabbi Eliezer said they would (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3).

sections.h: Ahaz and the settlers of Sepharvaim
sections.b: Ahaz "made his son pass through the fire" (2 Kings 16:3), which Chronicles describes as burning his sons in the Valley of Ben-hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:3). The verdict on Israel names the same sin (2 Kings 17:17), and the settlers from Sepharvaim burn their children to Adrammelech and Anammelech (2 Kings 17:31). The rabbis read "passing through the fire" as a rite of dedication rather than a killing (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7); most modern scholars think it was sacrifice.

Jehu destroys Baal but not "the gold calves that stood at Bethel and at Dan" (2 Kings 10:29), and almost every king of Israel after him is judged for "the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat" (2 Kings 13:2; 2 Kings 14:24; 2 Kings 15:9). The final verdict counts "a cast image, two calves" among the sins that brought Israel's exile (2 Kings 17:16, 21–22), and the priest sent back to teach the settlers lives at Bethel (2 Kings 17:28).

2 Kings 17:7–23 is the longest reflection by the narrator in Kings, built from Deuteronomy's language: fearing other gods, high places, standing stones, Asherah poles, stiff necks and rejected prophets. Most critical scholars assign it to the Deuteronomistic editors, with additions about Judah (2 Kings 17:13, 17:19–20) after 586 BC. Amaziah's obedience to Deuteronomy 24:16 (2 Kings 14:6) is another sign of the same school.

Athaliah's purge comes closer than anything before the exile to ending David's line. One infant, Joash, is saved and hidden in the temple, then crowned with David's spear and shields in the guards' hands (2 Kings 11:1–12). The promise that David would always have a lamp in Jerusalem survives through him.

Joash orders temple repairs, and when the priests fail to carry them out, Jehoiada sets a chest beside the altar so that the money goes straight to the workmen (2 Kings 12:4–16). Joash and Ahaz both strip the treasuries to pay foreign kings (2 Kings 12:18; 2 Kings 16:8). Ahaz builds a new altar on a Damascus model, moves the bronze altar aside, removes the panels of Solomon's stands and lowers the Sea from its bronze oxen (2 Kings 16:10–18).

"The LORD struck the king, and he had a skin disease until his dying day" (2 Kings 15:5). He lived in a separate house while his son Jotham governed. Kings gives no reason; Chronicles says the disease broke out on his forehead when he tried to burn incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

Jehoiada "cut a covenant" with the guards, and then made the covenant between the LORD, the king and the people (2 Kings 11:4, 17). The LORD spares Israel for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (2 Kings 13:23). At the end, Israel is condemned for rejecting "his covenant, the one he cut with their ancestors" (2 Kings 17:15), and the settlers are reminded of the covenant that forbids fearing other gods (2 Kings 17:35–38).

sections.h: "They went after vapor and became vapor"
sections.b: The verdict on Israel names the gods they served: Baal, the Asherah, the whole army of the sky, cast calves (2 Kings 17:16). It sums it up with a wordplay shared with Jeremiah 2:5: "They went after vapor and became vapor" (2 Kings 17:15). The settlers who replaced Israel "feared the LORD" while serving their own gods (2 Kings 17:33, 41), which Kings counts as not fearing him at all (2 Kings 17:34).

Jehu invites Jehonadab to "watch how zealous I am for the LORD" (2 Kings 10:16), claiming the zeal of Phinehas (Numbers 25:11–13) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:10). Hosea's judgment on "the blood of Jezreel" (Hosea 1:4) shows the Bible itself questioning such zeal.

Jehu kills Joram on the land of Naboth the Jezreelite and has his body thrown onto the plot, quoting an oracle that adds that Naboth's sons were killed too (2 Kings 9:21–26). The vineyard murder of 1 Kings 21 is paid back on the same ground.
